at se op til.explanation: "At se op til" means "to look up to". It is built from "at se" (to see), "op" (up) and "til" (to). To say you admire your mother, say: "Jeg ser op til min mor" (I look up to my mother).

at se på.explanation: "At se på" means "to look at". To say you look at the sky, say: "Han ser på himlen" (He looks at the sky). To say you search for something, use "at lede efter" (to look for): "Jeg leder efter min nøgle" (I am looking for my key).

at se tilbage.explanation: "At se tilbage" means "to look back". It is built from "at se" (to see) and "tilbage" (back). To say you turn your eyes behind you, say: "Hun så tilbage over skulderen" (She looked back over her shoulder).

at se tv.explanation: "At se tv" means "to watch TV". Danish uses "se" (to see) where English says "watch". To say you watch a movie, say: "Jeg ser en film" (I am watching a movie). The letters "tv" are said "te-ve".

at se ud.explanation: "At se ud" means "to look", as in how something appears. To say how a person seems, say: "Du ser træt ud" (You look tired). To ask what something looks like, say: "Hvordan ser det ud?" (What does it look like?) To look at something with your eyes, use "at se på" (to look at): "Jeg ser på billedet" (I look at the picture).

at sejle.explanation: "At sejle" means "to sail". To say you travel on water by boat, even with an engine, use the same verb: "Vi sejler til Sverige" (We are going to Sweden by boat). Rowing is "at ro" (to row): "Vi ror over søen" (We row across the lake).

at sende.explanation: "At sende" means "to send". To name the person right after the verb, say: "Jeg sender dig en besked" (I send you a message). To name the person after the item, add "til" (to): "Jeg sender en besked til dig" (I send a message to you).

at sende en sms.explanation: "At sende en sms" means "to text". It is literally "to send an SMS". To name the person you text, put "dig" (you) right after the verb: "Jeg sender dig en sms" (I send you a text).

at servere.explanation: "At servere" means "to serve", as in giving food or drink. To say you give guests something to eat and drink, say: "Vi serverer kaffe og kage" (We serve coffee and cake).

at shoppe.explanation: "At shoppe" means "to shop". It is borrowed from English. To say you buy groceries, use "at købe ind" (to buy groceries) instead: "Jeg køber ind til aftensmad" (I am buying groceries for dinner).

at sidde.explanation: "At sidde" means "to sit". To say where you sit, use "ved" (at): "Jeg sidder ved computeren" (I am sitting at the computer). To say you sit down, use "at sætte sig" (literally, to put oneself): "Jeg sætter mig" (I sit down).

at sidde fast.explanation: "At sidde fast" means "to be stuck". To say a key will not come out of a lock, say: "Nøglen sidder fast i låsen" (The key is stuck in the lock). To say you cannot go on with a task, say: "Jeg sidder fast med opgaven" (I am stuck on the task).

at sige.explanation: "At sige" means "to say". To ask what someone is saying, say: "Hvad siger du?" (What are you saying?) To tell a story, use "at fortælle" (to tell) instead: "Hun fortæller en historie" (She tells a story).

at sige farvel.explanation: "At sige farvel" means "to say goodbye". To say goodbye in a casual way, say: "Hej hej, vi ses!" (Bye bye, see you!)

at sige goddag.explanation: "At sige goddag" means "to say hello". It is literally "to say good day". To tell someone to say hi in a short way, use "hej" (hi): "Sig hej til din mor" (Say hi to your mother).

at sige op.explanation: "At sige op" means "to resign / quit". To say you leave your job, say: "Han sagde op i går" (He quit yesterday). To say you cancel a subscription, say: "Jeg sagde mit abonnement op" (I canceled my subscription).

at sige til.explanation: "At sige til" means "to tell / let know". To ask someone to let you know, say: "Sig til, hvis du har brug for hjælp" (Tell me if you need help). Without "til" (to), "at sige" means "to say": "Hun sagde hej" (She said hi).

at sige undskyld.explanation: "At sige undskyld" means "to say sorry". To get a stranger's attention, say "undskyld" by itself: "Undskyld, ved du, hvor stationen er?" (Excuse me, do you know where the station is?)

at signere.explanation: "At signere" means "to sign". To sign a form or a contract, use "at skrive under" (to sign a paper): "Du skal skrive under her" (You have to sign here). To say a player joins a club by contract, use "at signere": "Spilleren har signeret med klubben" (The player has signed with the club).

at sigte.explanation: "At sigte" means "to aim / charge". To say you point at what you want to hit, add "på" (at): "Han sigter på dåsen" (He aims at the can). To say the police officially suspect someone of a crime, say: "Han er sigtet for tyveri" (He is charged with theft).

at sikre.explanation: "At sikre" means "to secure / ensure". To say you fasten something so it stays safe, say: "Jeg sikrer cyklen med en lås" (I secure the bike with a lock). To say you make sure something happens, say: "Vi sikrer, at alle får mad" (We make sure everyone gets food). Do not mix it up with "at forsikre" (to insure): "Jeg forsikrer bilen" (I insure the car).

at simulere.explanation: "At simulere" means "to simulate". When you mean to pretend something that is not true, it means "to fake": "Han simulerer sygdom" (He is faking an illness).

at sjuske.explanation: "At sjuske" means "to be sloppy". To name the task you are sloppy with, add "med" (with) before the task: "sjuske med lektierne" (to be sloppy with the homework).

at skabe.explanation: "At skabe" means "to create". To say new jobs come into being, say: "skabe nye job" (to create new jobs). To say you make food, use "at lave" (to make) instead: "lave mad" (make food).

at skabe sig.explanation: "At skabe sig" means "to make a fuss". It is built from "at skabe" (to create) and "sig" (oneself), but it has nothing to do with creating. To say a child is making a fuss, say: "Barnet skaber sig i butikken" (The child is making a fuss in the shop).
